title: Pip and the Pantry Problem
markdown:
Consider the Emberfall peaks, rock the colour of a forgotten midnight, springs below breathing a warmth that kissed the cool air. Wizard Elden’s sturdy stone cottage sat among ancient volcanic slopes, spectacles usually a bit crooked, as if even glass preferred a tilt. He was a wizard of careful habits: ingredients in tiny neat writing, the cauldron polished daily until it shone like a captured star. The biscuit tin held exactly three honey-drizzled ginger snaps for emergencies, a census known only to Elden and to Biscuit — a jackdaw whose feathers kept a metallic gleam, whose clever eyes noticed the quill about to walk, the spectacles about to hide. Biscuit was not merely a pet. He was the nod before disaster.

This dawn the goal was sharp as ice: Moonpetal Moss, a delicate herb that bloomed only in the faintest pre-dawn, essential to the Sleepy Star potion, which promised dreams as peaceful as a sleeping badger. “Right then.” Elden adjusted the pointed hat with the frayed edge he always meant to mend with a special strong thread. “In and out, like a firefly at twilight. Linger and the morning dew will dampen more than moss.”

Biscuit’s caw was flint on a tiny hammer: the moss waits for no one.

Ash meadows crunched under leather. Sulphur and a sweetness like frost-kissed nuts. On the way back, satchel already comfortably mossy, Elden heard a squeak small enough to be wind. Under a black boulder sat a creature his mountain notes had not budgeted for: round, impossibly fluffy, humming from the middle like a happy engine, a dandelion that had forgotten flight.

“Hello.” Carefulness stepped aside. He knelt, moss-green on his fingers. The loaf-sized puff wiggled closer, liquid eyes doing their work. “Not quite right, little one. Far from home?”

Biscuit, on the shoulder, did not caw. That was his deep-thought face.

Elden scooped. Warm as a sunned stone, hum louder. “Night owls. Bolder winds. We cannot leave you.”

Home gained a companion. He called it Pip, a name as plain as a good blanket. Pip loved warmth, soft piles, the hum of being allowed. By the hearth Pip became a living ember against the dramatic windows.

The next day the pantry showed its empty corners. Dried cloudberries, useful against small sadnesses, were especially gone. Pip travelled in an extra-fluffy blanket in the satchel; Biscuit kept the air above. The Warm Springs Inn was the mountain’s gossip and stew in one room: prospectors, merchants, scholars of rare dirt. Martha the innkeeper had a laugh that tested rafters and a heart to match the springs.

“Martha. Cloudberries, if you have them, and yesterday’s ash-root stew if it survived.”

She wiped flour on her apron. “Elden. I didn’t expect you for that question today. Later in the week, I thought.”

Spectacles slid. “Question? Are the berries shy this season?”

“The Fuzzyfoot Fluff.” A stage whisper that reached half the room. “Old Silas at the forge says you’re the only one who can name it. His prize goat sheds like a summer storm. Bare as a winter branch.”

Elden’s mind offered charms, potions, warmth, small repairs — not veterinary myth. Cheeks went unmagical pink. “Tricky. I’ll need the books. Point me at Silas’s goat; I’ll look and suggest.” He hoped the detour would also produce cloudberries.

Meanwhile Biscuit, who had claimed a high dusty beam over the common room, overheard Martha to a stout grey-bearded patron. That jackdaw of Elden’s, a nuisance, always eyeing the counter’s shine; without that blasted bird the best silver spoons would still be here, not scattered through the valley like fallen leaves. Biscuit’s eyes narrowed to slits. He knew, with a seasoned observer’s certainty, that the timing of the complaint fitted the new puff — currently dozing in wool, arrived yesterday — and not a bird who had lived above this room for years. Loyalty surged, fierce and slightly aimed at the wrong target. Pip needed his name cleared. Real shiny treasures, perhaps, to soothe an innkeeper. A determined glint. A beak-nudge into the satchel. Caw. Caw. Shiny. Urgency, he hoped, translated.

Pip, nestled in Elden’s arms after a reshuffle of blanket, felt the insistent tug and the inn’s tide of talk. Warm hearths. Safe nests. Winter burrows. Being a creature who sought the cosiest honest place, he heard a warning. The inn might force a hide in some inadequate exposed spot, or worse, a burrow dug through tough earth and stone. The thought of cold hard wall, to a body used to soft naps, was a kind of horror. He had to leave this dangerous warmth for a proper one. He spotted a promisingly soft section of pantry wall, lined with plump flour sacks, yeast and comfort on the air — much more inviting than stone.

Climax arrived as climaxes do: flour, noise, crossed wires. Elden had the berries and the stew and was leaving quietly when Pip, taking a large whisk for a digging tool, excavated the pantry with earnest joy. A white weather hid him. Martha saw the hole in her stores. “The pest! Shoo, fluffy fiend!” Then Biscuit at a dropped silver thimble, pecking with purpose. “And the bird! A pair!”

Silas stomped in, soot on the apron, anger on the face. “Martha! The prize goat’s gone. I saw Elden’s fluffy thing this way. Fuzzyfoot Fuzz. Irresistible to goats.”

Elden stood in it: Pip blinking flour, Biscuit pleased with a thimble, Silas sputtering livestock. The messy, unplanned knot he disliked most. Then he looked again. Pip shivered from confusion, not cold. Biscuit’s help was loyal and aimed at the wrong shiny. Silas’s anger was a missing goat, not meanness.

“Hold.” Steady, a bell through the room. “Martha, Pip is a Hummie-Puff. Warmth, not spoons, and no talent for trouble. Biscuit—” he took the thimble; a sheepish caw — “finds what is lost and calls it treasure. Silas, your goat is not here. Pip, you are not in danger. The inn is warm. You may rest without digging.”

He untangled the rest with patience that did not need a wand. Pip learned a hearth could be asked for. Biscuit offered the thimble as if it were an apology that happened to be silver. Martha, flustered, still smiled at a floury face. Silas grumbled about fences; the anger left the room first.

Cottage again. Pip hummed on new cushions. Biscuit preened, smug, and rolled a polished grey pebble to Elden — a peace-offering from the inn floor, meaning well. Elden set it on the mantel and did not announce that he had navigated a social storm. The moss waited in its jar. The snaps in the tin were still three.

The next evening the village did Hearthwarming: lanterns on the paths, a lute that knew four honest notes, roasting nuts, talk. Elden sat with Pip a warm weight on his lap and Biscuit on the shoulder that had always been a perch. He remained a wizard who liked things just so. He also knew, without saying it to the peaks, that a hearth holds more than a potion. Silas, across the fire, nodded once about a goat that had been in the next meadow all along. Martha sent over a spoon that was not silver and not missing. Pip’s hum kept time with the lute, badly, which was fine.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
